tips: Turn off the tap while brushing, shaving or washing your face. When you replace a faucet aerator, EPCOR says to choose one under 4.7 L/min or labelled WaterSense.
Take a shower instead of a bath. Five minutes is the ideal shower EPCOR names, and cutting a shower by 2 minutes makes a noticeable difference. A WaterSense shower head is under 7.0 L/min.
Check the toilet for leaks with food colouring in the tank (colour in the bowl after 15–20 minutes means a leak). A replacement toilet should use 4.8 litres or less per flush.
Check faucets, pipes, taps and hoses for drips. EPCOR says a hardware store can fix most minor leaks.

quality.h1: Water quality in Edmonton and Alberta
quality.lead: What's in Edmonton's tap water, what to watch for on a private well, and how to get your water tested. Every number comes from the official page linked under it. Want your own water checked?
quality.cta_text: Hard-water scale, a funny taste, an older home with possible lead pipes, or a well? Send a request and we'll follow up.

sections.heading: Edmonton tap water (EPCOR)
sections.intro: EPCOR treats water from the North Saskatchewan River at two plants, E.L. Smith and Rossdale, and supplies Edmonton and much of the region. EPCOR publishes daily and monthly test results.

cards.title: Hardness: hard, about 165–180 mg/L
cards.html: EPCOR says the river water is moderately hard, about 165 mg/L as calcium carbonate on average, from minerals picked up flowing over limestone. Its June 2026 summary averaged 168 mg/L at the treatment plants, ranging 153–186. On Alberta Health's scale, 120–180 mg/L counts as "hard" (about 10 grains per gallon). Hardness has no health guideline. It causes scale on kettles, fixtures and water heaters, and you'll need more soap.

cards.title: Disinfectant: chloramine, about 2 mg/L
cards.html: The chlorine in Edmonton's pipes is all chloramine, which is chlorine combined with ammonia. It's weaker than free chlorine but lasts longer in the pipes. EPCOR's approval allows 0.5–2.5 mg/L, and June 2026 averaged 2.07 mg/L. If you keep fish, chloramine has to be removed from aquarium water.

cards.title: Fluoride: about 0.7 mg/L
cards.html: EPCOR targets 0.60–0.80 mg/L of fluoride. June 2026 averaged 0.67 mg/L, under Health Canada's 1.5 mg/L limit.

cards.title: Lead service lines in older homes
cards.html: Some older homes are still connected by a lead service line. EPCOR has been replacing them since 2008 and adds orthophosphate to the water to reduce lead release. EPCOR owns the pipe from the main to the property line, and the owner is responsible from the property line to the meter. If you have or suspect a lead line, EPCOR offers free annual lead testing and a free NSF-53 certified filter on request: 780-412-6858 or leadmanagement@epcor.com. Health Canada's limit for lead is 5 µg/L. Drink and cook only with cold tap water.

sources.label: EPCOR: Lead and your drinking water

cards.title: Spring runoff taste and smell
cards.html: Each spring, snowmelt carries soil and plant material into the river, so tap water can taste or smell earthy, musty or more like chlorine for a few weeks. EPCOR says it stays safe to drink and adjusts treatment, for example with powdered activated carbon. Running the cold tap, chilling the water or using a carbon filter helps.

cards.title: Other results
cards.html: EPCOR's June 2026 summary shows nitrate around 0.1 mg/L (limit 10), arsenic at 0.0002 mg/L or less (limit 0.01), iron under 0.005 mg/L, and sodium around 12–14 mg/L. Anyone on a sodium-restricted diet should know that a water softener adds sodium.

sections.heading: Private wells in Alberta
sections.intro: If your water comes from a well, cistern or dugout, nobody tests it for you. The owner is responsible for keeping it safe.

cards.title: Free testing through Alberta Health Services
cards.html: AHS Environmental Public Health tests private drinking water supplies for bacteria (total coliform and E. coli) and for chemicals and trace metals. Pick up approved bottles at your local public health centre. AHS says to test for bacteria twice a year and for chemistry every 3 years. Some centres charge a small shipping fee. AHS won't test for real estate, farm or business purposes, and it doesn't test city water.

sources.label: MyHealth Alberta: Testing your drinking water
AHS: free testing for private drinking water

cards.title: When to test
cards.html: Test in spring after the snow melts, after a dry spell, heavy rain or flooding, after pump repairs, if the taste, colour or smell changes, when you move in, and before a baby arrives.

sources.label: Alberta Working Well: Taking water samples (PDF)

cards.title: Common well-water issues
cards.html:
• Hardness: scale and extra soap use. 180 mg/L or more counts as very hard. Softeners add sodium or potassium.
  • Iron: over 0.3 mg/L causes reddish-brown stains and a metal taste, and can feed iron bacteria.
  • Nitrate: the limit is 10 mg/L as nitrate-N. High levels are a risk for babies. Boiling makes it worse. Use reverse osmosis or distillation.
  • Arsenic: occurs naturally from rock in some areas. The limit is 0.01 mg/L.
